title: I Let a Student Back In After Everyone Told Me Not To
author: Larry J. Walsh
summary: Principal Larry J. Walsh recounts overriding a district hearing officer's recommendation and reinstating a student who had been expelled under a mandatory weapons rule. He explains that a close reading of counseling notes from the student's alternative placement revealed consistent attendance, a strong mentor relationship and an unusually self-aware personal statement, and that he brought the placement counselor into the review to testify directly. Walsh is candid about the cost: two assistant principals and many staff believed he was making an emotional decision, and one worried most about the precedent it would set. The piece shows how he structured the risk, with a re-entry plan, twice-weekly counseling check-ins and a probation period that any serious incident would end. Six months later the student had no incidents, better grades and attendance, and asked to speak to incoming ninth graders. Walsh distills a transferable principle for school leaders: a file read only for risk misses evidence of change, and an override should rest on evidence plus built-in structure rather than optimism.
points: Walsh found no precedent in five years of district files for a principal overriding a readmission recommendation, underscoring how rarely the authority is used.
He brought the alternative placement counselor into the review by phone so the hearing officer heard firsthand evidence rather than a secondhand reading of the file.
Reinstatement came with explicit conditions: a structured re-entry plan, twice-weekly counselor check-ins and a probation period with a clear line for ending the arrangement.
He acknowledges that second chances cost a leader credibility before they earn anything back, and that he signed before knowing the outcome.
The closing principle holds that reviewing a file for the whole person can surface genuine change that a risk-only review misses.
quotes: I asked the hearing officer for the chance to override the recommendation, which is within my authority as principal but rarely exercised, rarely enough that I could not find a precedent in our district’s files from the previous five years.
Two of my assistant principals told me directly, that they thought I was making an emotional decision that would put other students at risk.

I signed the reinstatement anyway, with conditions: a structured re-entry plan, a check-in with a counselor twice a week for the first semester, and a probationary period during which any serious incident would end the arrangement immediately and permanently.
One assistant principal told me, months later, that what had bothered her most at the time was not the decision itself but the precedent it might set.
I try to remember that credibility spent on a decision that works out is easier to recover than the version where it does not, and that I signed the paperwork before I knew which version I would get.

Reading them side by side is the closest thing I have to proof that a single incident does not have to be the last word on a kid, provided someone is willing to read the whole file and not just the worst page of it.
But a file reviewed only for risk will miss evidence of genuine change that a file reviewed for the whole person can surface.
